nodes.title: Machine learning fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Machine learning lets computers learn patterns from data without explicit programming. Azure AI-900 exams test the four core ML task types, the train/validate/test split, and which Azure service handles each scenario.

flashcards.front: Four types of machine learning workloads?
flashcards.back: Regression (predict a number), Classification (predict a category), Clustering (group unlabelled data), Anomaly detection (find outliers).

flashcards.front: What is the role of a validation set?
flashcards.back: Tune hyperparameters and catch overfitting during training — separate from the test set, which is only touched once to report final accuracy.

flashcards.front: Deep learning vs classical ML — key difference?
flashcards.back: Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks that learn features automatically; classical ML requires manual feature engineering.

flashcards.front: Azure Machine Learning vs Azure AI Services?
flashcards.back: Azure ML is for training and deploying custom models; Azure AI Services are pre-built APIs (Vision, Speech, Language) — no training required.

questions.q: Which type of machine learning is used to predict a continuous numeric value, such as the future selling price of a house from its features?
questions.explanation: Regression is a supervised learning technique that predicts a continuous numeric value (price, temperature, demand) by learning a function from labelled examples. Classification is also supervised but returns a discrete class label — it would only bucket the house into a price band, not produce a precise value. Unsupervised clustering groups unlabelled data by similarity and never produces a numeric target prediction. Reinforcement learning learns a policy by trial and error against environment rewards, which does not fit a static "features → target price" supervised setup.

questions.q: An online retailer wants to automatically segment shoppers by purchase behaviour when no category labels are available. Which machine-learning approach is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Clustering is the unsupervised technique that groups items by feature similarity when no labels are provided — k-means partitions into a fixed k of centroids, DBSCAN discovers density-based clusters and marks noise. Supervised classification cannot run at all without labelled training data, so it is unusable on an unlabelled shopper population. Regression is also supervised and predicts a continuous number rather than assigning group membership. Anomaly detection isolates rare outlier records against a normal baseline rather than partitioning the entire population into interpretable segments.

questions.q: A model scores very high on its training data but performs poorly on new, unseen samples. What is this behaviour called?
questions.explanation: Overfitting means the model has memorised the training data (including its noise) and fails to generalise to unseen examples — the classic "good on train, bad on test" split. Mitigations include collecting more training data, regularisation, simpler models, cross-validation and early stopping. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple and scores poorly on both training and test sets. Class imbalance is a skewed label distribution that biases predictions toward the majority class, but it does not by itself cause a train/test gap. Data drift is a shift in the input distribution after deployment — a post-deployment monitoring problem, not a train-vs-test-set behaviour.

questions.q: On a strongly imbalanced binary-classification problem such as credit-card fraud detection, which metric gives the most informative view of model quality?
questions.explanation: F1-score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, is the standard classification metric on strongly imbalanced problems because it penalises both missed positives and false alarms; precision–recall curves and AUC-PR are common companions. Plain classification accuracy is misleading — predicting "not fraud" for every row still yields >99% accuracy on typical fraud data while catching zero fraud. MAE measures absolute error against a continuous target and applies to regression, not to a discrete positive/negative label. R-squared measures the fraction of variance explained by a regression model — also a regression metric, not a classification one.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.
